blocks.text: A BST can be walked in the same four orders as any binary tree — but in a BST each order **means** something. The most important: an **in-order** walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) visits the values in **sorted order**, because everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is bigger. Half of all BST interview questions are this one fact in disguise.

blocks.alt: The tree with root 8 and its four traversals. In-order gives 1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14, sorted. Pre-order gives 8 3 1 6 4 7 10 14 13, which rebuilds the same tree. Post-order gives 1 4 7 6 3 13 14 10 8, children before parents. Level order gives 8 3 10 1 6 14 4 7 13, top to bottom.

blocks.text: What each order is for in a BST

items: **In-order** — the values smallest first: k-th smallest, validating a BST, merging two BSTs, "two sum" on a BST. Walk **right, node, left** instead (reverse in-order) to get them largest first.
**Pre-order** — a node comes before its subtrees, so inserting the pre-order sequence into an empty BST **rebuilds the exact same tree**. That's how a BST is copied or serialized.
**Post-order** — children before their parent: free a tree, or compute something that needs both subtrees first (size, height, "is this subtree a BST?").
**Level order** — one depth at a time, with a queue: print the tree by levels, or find the minimum depth.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h)** for the call stack.

The recursion's call stack can be made explicit: go **left as far as possible**, pushing every node on the way; pop one, visit it, then do the same from its **right** child. The stack always holds the nodes still waiting for their turn — at most one per level. This version can also be **paused** after any value, which is exactly what the BST Iterator problem needs.

blocks.caption: Push the whole left spine, pop and visit, then continue from the right child.

blocks.code:
def inorder(root):
    out, stack = [], []
    node = root
    while node is not None or stack:
        while node is not None:           # go left as far as possible,
            stack.append(node)            # remembering each node on the way
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()                # the smallest value not visited yet
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.right                 # then everything just bigger than it
    return out

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h).** Every node is pushed once and popped once.
3. Morris traversal: no stack at all

Morris traversal visits in-order with **O(1)** extra memory by borrowing the tree's own empty pointers. Before going left from a node, find its **predecessor** (the rightmost node of its left subtree) and point that node's empty `right` at the current node — a temporary thread back up. When the walk later reaches the thread, it knows the left side is done: it removes the thread, visits the node and goes right. The tree ends up exactly as it started.
**Time O(n), space O(1).** Each edge is walked at most a few times while finding predecessors, so it's still linear. It temporarily changes the tree, so it isn't safe while another thread reads it.
These are written exactly as for any binary tree — the Binary Tree course walks through each with a simulator. In short:

blocks.code:
pre-order:   visit(node); walk(node.left); walk(node.right)
post-order:  walk(node.left); walk(node.right); visit(node)
level order: a queue: pop a node, visit it, push its children
